paper_title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion and flow-based models have become leading paradigms for visual generative modeling, driven by rapid advances in algorithm designs and model architectures. Early diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021) operate directly on pixels with classical U-Nets (Ronneberger et al., 2015), but struggle with efficiency and fidelity at high resolutions. To alleviate this difficulty, latent diffusion moves denoising from pixel space to compact latent space produced by separately trained autoencoder (Rombach et al., 2022). Combined with the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture (Peebles & Xie, 2023), this formulation has become standard design for high-resolution visual generation. Despite its efficiency, latent diffusion is inherently bounded by the autoencoder, including reconstruction error (Yu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026), additional training and inference costs (Leng et al., 2025; Cheng & Yuan, 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), and limited cross-modal capability for joint modeling (Bounoua et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Thus recent works revisit pixel-space diffusion and demonstrate competitive quality on image generation (Li & He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). In contrast, video generation is still dominated by latent DiTs (Ma et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025), while pixel-space models mostly retain U-Net-style skip connections (Gu et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025) or cascaded generation (Menapace et al., 2024; Skorokhodov et al., 2024). This motivates us to investigate how far simple DiT-style Transformer can go in direct pixel-space video generation. We introduce JVT, pixel-space video generative model built on simple DiT-style Transformer backbone, without detailers, cascaded stages or U-Net-style skip connections. Following JiT (Li & He, 2026), JVT predicts clean videos from noisy pixels under rectified-flow objective. To make raw videos tractable, we explore variants of video patch embedding for efficient spatiotemporal downsampling. We further examine the design choices of register tokens (Darcet et al., 2024) and adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) (Peebles & Xie, 2023), which can carry noise level or class condition and amplify it by register guidance (Starodubcev et al., 2026) or classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021). With these design choices, JVT achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. Pixel-space video modeling also provides direct interface for jointly generating video and pixelaligned modalities, which typically requires reusing an RGB-specific autoencoder in latent diffusion (Ke et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a). We extend JVT to camera-conditioned joint RGB-disparity generation to demonstrate this cross-modal capability. Without an additional reconstruction model at inference, the generated disparity yields sequence of point clouds in world coordinates, which enables explicit 4D world modeling. Experiments further show that joint RGBdisparity generation improves camera following relative to RGB-only JVT. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We present JVT, the first pixel-space video diffusion model built on simple DiT-style Transformer backbone, without detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically study video patch embeddings and conditioning mechanisms, identifying designs that improve the quality-efficiency trade-off. In class-conditioned and unconditional settings, JVT achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines. We formulate pixel-aligned joint generation as native extension of JVT. We further demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity video generation, which enables explicit 4D scene representation and improves camera following relative to RGB-only generation.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: High-resolution pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion modeling for high-resolution visual data has long relied on specialized architectures, including cascaded diffusion (Ho et al., 2022a; Teng et al., 2024), cross-resolution designs (Gu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b), multiscale or U-shaped backbones (Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Crowson et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026), frequency decomposition (Ma et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a), and 2 auxiliary detail modules (Wang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). Though effective, these approaches often introduce additional architectural or training complexity, which can limit efficiency and scalability. Recently, JiT (Li & He, 2026) achieves high-resolution image generation competitive with latent diffusion using simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer. This paradigm is also extended to one-step image generation (Lu et al., 2026) and text-to-image generation (Wang et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026), further demonstrating the effectiveness. Video Transformer architectures. Modern video Transformers largely retain the standard blocks of 2D Vision Transformers (ViTs), making patch embedding the key adaptation to video inputs (Tong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025). common choice is tubelet embedding (Arnab et al., 2021), which encodes non-overlapping spatiotemporal patches into tokens via 3D convolution. This architecture is also widely adopted in latent video DiTs, whereas pixel-space video diffusion methods still typically rely on U-shaped architectures (Gu et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Hoogeboom et al., 2025) or cascaded generation (Menapace et al., 2024; Skorokhodov et al., 2024). Our work aims to explore whether simple DiT-style video Transformer can also support direct pixel-space video generation.

Spatiotemporal factorization. Inspired by the factorization principle of depthwise separable convolution (Chollet, 2017; Howard et al., 2017), we separate the spatial and temporal operations of tubelet embedding. sections.title: 3.4 PIXEL-ALIGNED JOINT GENERATION
sections.content: Pixel-aligned signals about geometry, motion, and semantic structure provide complementary cues for video generation. By channel-wise concatenating RGB frames with these signals (Ke et al., 2024), diffusion models can jointly generate RGB content and spatially aligned auxiliary modalities (Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026a). Pixel-space modeling allows these modalities to be represented on shared spatiotemporal grid without an RGB-specific autoencoder. After modality-specific normalization, we concatenate an RGB video xrgb RT 3HW with pixel-aligned modalities along the channel dimension: x0 = [xrgb; x(1); . . . ; x(M )] RT CjointHW , (6) where x(m) RT CmHW denotes the m-th aligned modality and Cjoint = 3 + (cid:80)M m=1 Cm is the total number of channels. These modalities may include depth, surface normals, ray maps, segmentation masks, and optical flow. All modalities share the same noise level and are predicted jointly during denoising. We instantiate this formulation with RGB and disparity, reparameterization of depth, for cameraconditioned video generation (Sec. 4.3). At inference, we convert the predicted disparity back to depth and unproject it using the camera parameters. Combined with the generated RGB frames, this yields sequence of colored point clouds without an additional reconstruction model.

sections.content: 4.1 MAIN RESULTS Datasets. For class-conditioned generation and unconditional generation, we conduct experiments on four datasets: UCF-101 (Soomro et al., 2012), FaceForensics (Rossler et al., 2018), SkyTimelapse (Xiong et al., 2018), and Taichi-HD (Siarohin et al., 2019). Following settings of previous works (Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2025), we use both training and test splits of UCF-101, and only the training split of the other datasets. We randomly extract 16-frame video clips with frame interval of 3, and resize all video frames to 256 256 resolution for training. Evaluation metrics. We evaluate generation quality with Frechet Video Distance (FVD) (Unterthiner et al., 2019), using 2,048 generated samples. For efficiency metrics, we report parameter count, floating point operations (FLOPs), peak allocated GPU memory and inference latency. Additional details about these metrics are given in Appendix (A.2, A.4). Baselines. Our main baseline is Latte (Ma et al., 2025), representative DiT-based latent diffusion model. Other competing methods include GAN-based methods (Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022), autoregressive models (Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024a), U-Net-based latent diffusion (He et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023b) and DiT-based latent diffusion (Liu et al., 2024). Given an initial RGB frame and target camera trajectory, we jointly generate RGB frames and aligned disparity maps. After recovering depth from disparity, the camera parameters allow the predictions to be unprojected into sequence of colored point clouds, providing an explicit 4D representation of the generated scene, as shown in Fig. 5. Experimental setting. We conduct 8-frame camera-conditioned video generation experiments on RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018) at resolution of 256 256. As dense depth annotations are unavailable, frozen lightweight 3D reconstruction model, Pi3X (Wang et al., 2026d) supplies depth targets online during training. Following prior works (Song et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025), we reversibly transform depth to square-root disparity = (D + 1)1/2 and concatenate it with RGB as four-channel target. Evaluation. We evaluate RGB video quality using FVD, and assess camera following by comparing Pi3X-estimated relative poses with the target camera trajectory. Following prior works (Wang et al., 2024b; 2025a; 2026d), we report relative rotation accuracy (RRA), relative translation accuracy (RTA), and AUC as camera-following metrics. Specifically, RRA and RTA measure the percentages of evaluated frame pairs whose rotation and translation-direction errors fall below given threshold, respectively, while AUC summarizes their joint error distribution. We use thresholds of 5 and 30. We compare JVT with pixel-space U-ViT models (Song et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026) and latentspace DiT (Huang et al., 2026b). As shown in Tab. 5, both JVT variants achieve lower FVD than these baselines. Joint RGB-disparity generation achieves the highest RTA and AUC among all compared methods, with only slight increase in FVD relative to RGB-only JVT. The qualitative results in Fig. 6 further illustrate the differences in camera following. Across methods, RRA is consistently high, whereas RTA remains substantially lower. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We demonstrate pixel-space video generation with simple DiT-style Transformer, achieving generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional video generation benchmarks. Our ablations study suggests patch-first embedding for spatiotemporal tokenization and standard AdaLN for conditioning. For the register mechanism, register-free JVT provides an acceptable baseline, while register guidance can offer additional gains, particularly on the more diverse UCF-101 dataset. Pixel-space modeling makes pixel-aligned joint generation straightforward by representing RGB and aligned modalities on common spatiotemporal grid, without encoding them into shared pretrained latent space. When extending JVT to camera-conditioned joint RGB-disparity generation, we find camera following is improved relative to RGB-only baselines, with small FVD trade-off. These findings highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video generation and pixel-aligned joint modeling. We hope our empirical findings help guide future efforts to scale pixel-space video generation to larger model size, more datasets, longer videos and higher resolutions.

As shown in Fig. 4, the register mechanism brings clear gains on UCF-101 but only limited benefits on the other datasets, so we use register tokens only for class-conditioned and unconditional video generation on UCF-101. The register initialization ablation in Tab. 3 further shows no gain from injecting the timestep or class embedding into the register tokens, and we therefore just set er = 0 when registers are used. The base registers R0 are learnable tokens initialized i.i.d. from zero-mean Gaussian with standard deviation 0.02. All register-equipped variants are sampled with register guidance, whose scale is selected by linear search with step size of 0.1. Training details. All models are trained from scratch. Following JiT (Li & He, 2026), we use clean data prediction and velocity MSE loss. For noise sampling, we sample noise level tbase from logit-normal distribution (Esser et al., 2024) and shift it with noise shift s, as shown in Eq. (7). Our full-scale training of JVT use global batch size of 256 with 8 NVIDIA 80GB GPUs, while some ablations use batch size of 40 on single GPU  (Fig. 7)  . = tbase 1 + (s 1) tbase (7) For camera-conditioned generation, we sample the video noise independently for each frame, following DFoT (Song et al., 2025). We also adopt the data augmentations of the DFoT dataloader: horizontal flipping and temporal reversal, each applied with probability 0.5, and back-and-forth augmentation with probability 0.1. 18 Sampling configurations. Tab. 7 specifies the exact sampling configuration of each main result. We use the Euler solver for class-conditioned and camera-conditioned generation, and the Heun solver for unconditional generation. All samplers run for 50 denoising steps, with the timestep schedule shifted by the noise shift (Eq. (7)). Depending on the task, we apply classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2021), register guidance (RG) (Starodubcev et al., 2026), or history guidance (HG) (Song et al., 2025). The CFG scale is selected by linear search with step size of 1, and the RG scale with step size of 0.1. For FVD evaluation, we generate 2,048 clips per method and use the same number of real clips as the reference. Geometry annotation for RealEstate10K. As in Sec. 4.3, dense depth annotations are unavailable for RealEstate10K, so we use frozen Pi3X (Wang et al., 2026d) to supply depth pseudo-labels online during training. For each training clip, Pi3X is conditioned on the prescribed camera intrinsics and extrinsics as priors. Since Pi3X predicts scale-invariant geometry and affine-invariant cameras, we estimate the global scale of the predicted depth by aligning the predicted cameras with the ground-truth cameras. The aligned depth is clamped to minimum of 105 and, following prior works (Song et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025), reversibly transformed to square-root disparity = (D + 1)1/2, which is concatenated with RGB as four-channel target.
